title: What are @Embeddable and @Embedded in JPA? How do they model value objects, and how do you use @AttributeOverride when the same embeddable type appears twice in one entity?

s1_definition.profdef: `@Embeddable` marks a class whose fields are stored inline as columns of the owning entity's table rather than in a separate table — it has no identity of its own and represents a **value object** (defined by its values, not by an id). `@Embedded` marks a field in an entity that holds an instance of that embeddable, so its columns are merged into the entity's table. When the same embeddable type is used twice in one entity (for example a home `Address` and an office `Address`), both would map to the same column names and clash, so `@AttributeOverride` (and `@AttributeOverrides`) renames each embeddable's columns to keep them distinct.
s1_definition.analogy: A value object is like a customer's address — it has no account number of its own; it only matters as a bundle of street, city, and pincode attached to the customer. `@Embeddable` says "address is a reusable bundle," and `@Embedded` says "stamp that bundle's fields directly onto the customer's record" rather than keeping a separate address file. But if a customer has both a home address and an office address, and both bundles want to write to columns named street, city, and pincode, the two would collide on the same record. `@AttributeOverride` is the instruction "for the office bundle, write to office_street, office_city, office_pincode instead" so both fit on one record.
s1_definition.oneliner: @Embeddable = value object stored inline; @Embedded = include it in the entity's table; @AttributeOverride renames columns so the same embeddable can appear twice without clashing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `@Embeddable` marks a class whose fields are stored inline as columns of the owning entity's table rather than in a separate table — it has no identity of its own and represents a **value object** (defined by its values, not by an id). `@Embedded` marks a field in an entity that holds an instance of that embeddable, so its columns are merged into the entity's table. When the same embeddable type is used twice in one entity (for example a home `Address` and an office `Address`), both would map to the same column names and clash, so `@AttributeOverride` (and `@AttributeOverrides`) renames each embeddable's columns to keep them distinct.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A value object is like a customer's address — it has no account number of its own; it only matters as a bundle of street, city, and pincode attached to the customer. `@Embeddable` says "address is a reusable bundle," and `@Embedded` says "stamp that bundle's fields directly onto the customer's record" rather than keeping a separate address file. But if a customer has both a home address and an office address, and both bundles want to write to columns named street, city, and pincode, the two would collide on the same record. `@AttributeOverride` is the instruction "for the office bundle, write to office_street, office_city, office_pincode instead" so both fit on one record.

**One line to remember:** @Embeddable = value object stored inline; @Embedded = include it in the entity's table; @AttributeOverride renames columns so the same embeddable can appear twice without clashing.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — money was modelled as a loose BigDecimal plus a separate currency string, and they drifted apart.** At National Bank of India, amount and currency were stored as unrelated fields and sometimes a rupee amount got tagged with the wrong currency. Bundling them into a `Money` value object with invariants keeps them together. This is exactly what an embeddable value object provides.

**Problem 2 — a customer needs both a home and an office address on one record.** Both addresses have the same shape, so embedding the same `Address` type twice collides on column names. This is exactly what `@AttributeOverride` resolves.

What the code will do: an `Account` entity embedding a `Money` balance value object, and a `Customer` entity embedding `Address` twice (home and office) with `@AttributeOverride`, plus a service that builds and reads them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: onboard Rajesh with a Money balance and both home and office addresses.

Step 1 — the service constructs a Money value object (amount plus currency, with a currency invariant) and two Address value objects, one home and one office.

Step 2 — these value objects are set on the Customer entity. They have no ids of their own; they are just bundles of fields.

Step 3 — `save(c)` issues a single INSERT into customers. The Money fields map to balance_amount and balance_currency; the home Address maps to street, city, pincode; and because of `@AttributeOverride`, the office Address maps to office_street, office_city, office_pincode in the same row.

Step 4 — there is no join and no separate address table; all the embeddable columns live inline, so reading the customer reads everything in one row.

Step 5 — when loaded back, Hibernate reconstructs the Money and both Address objects from the respective columns, and equals on the value objects compares by value, so two addresses with identical fields are equal.


sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — @Embeddable Value Objects (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Value Object (DDD): identity-less, immutable, equals by value│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Money owns currency invariant; Customer owns identity   │
  │  O: reuse Address anywhere by embedding + overriding columns│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ Customer (@Entity)        │
  │ - id: String  @Id         │
  │ - balance: Money  @Embedded          ◆ owns VO
  │ - homeAddress: Address @Embedded     ◆ (default cols)
  │ - officeAddress: Address @Embedded   ◆ @AttributeOverride(office_*)
  └─────────────┬─────────────┘
         embeds ▼                  embeds ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Money (@Embeddable)  │   │ Address (@Embeddable)    │
  │ - amount, currency   │   │ - street, city, pincode  │
  │ + add(Money)         │   │ equals/hashCode by value │
  │ equals by value      │   └──────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘

  ── Column Mapping (as prose) ──
  Money → balance_amount, balance_currency.
  homeAddress → street, city, pincode (defaults).
  officeAddress → office_street, office_city, office_pincode (overridden).

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. build Money + 2 Address VOs  2. set on Customer
  3. save → single INSERT (all inline)  4. load → reconstruct VOs

  (Caution) same embeddable twice without @AttributeOverride → column clash.
  (Caution) embeddables load eagerly with the entity (no lazy). (Caution) all-null = "no value".
  Rule: model identity-less bundles as immutable @Embeddable; override columns to reuse.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The embeddable annotation marks a class whose fields are stored inline as columns of the owning entity's table rather than in a separate table, and it represents a value object, meaning something defined purely by its values and having no identity of its own, like money, an address, or a date range. The embedded annotation marks the field in the entity that holds an instance of that embeddable, so its columns are merged into the entity's own table with no join and no separate id. Modeling these as value objects keeps the domain clean, because I can have a reusable money type that enforces its own invariant that an amount and a currency always travel together, while the database just sees plain columns.

The interesting case is embedding the same type twice in one entity, such as a home address and an office address that are both the same address shape. By default both embeddeds map to the same column names, street, city, and pincode, which collides on a single row. The attribute override annotation, and its plural form, renames one or both so, for example, the office address writes to office street, office city, and office pincode while the home address keeps the default names, and now both fit in the same table.

At National Bank of India I used an embeddable money type to fix a real bug where an amount and its currency were stored as loose, unrelated fields and sometimes drifted apart, tagging a rupee amount with the wrong currency; bundling them into a value object with a currency invariant made that impossible. I also had a customer who needed both a home and an office address on one record, and I embedded the same address type twice with attribute overrides on the office columns. The nuances I always mention are that value objects should be immutable with equals and hashCode based on all their fields so two equal bundles compare equal, that embeddables can be nested and overrides can reach nested paths, that an embedded value loads eagerly with the entity because it shares the table, and that I take care to distinguish a completely null embedded value, meaning no address, from an address whose individual fields happen to be null.

---

keyPoints: @Embeddable: value object class — no own identity, no own table
@Embedded: use an embeddable inside an entity
Fields of embeddable stored in the entity table
@AttributeOverride: rename columns when reusing same embeddable
